Xiao Shen stared blankly at the scene before remembering the mission he’d forgotten.
“Base.
Base, respond.”
*Chhh.*
Static hissed from the radio enchanted with communication magic as it sent out a mana-laced signal.
The signal pushed through the unstable magical power permeating the air, traveling farther and farther.
And when Xiao Shen’s urgent transmission finally reached the main force—
“Company, halt!”
An aircraft carrying someone landed smoothly on the runway, between ranks of soldiers and Hunters standing in flawless formation.
This operation involved a hundred thousand Hunters and a coalition of nations from across the world.
It was massive—less an operation than a war.
Plenty of Hunters remained at the main base, and there were so many soldiers you could hardly take a step without running into one.
An army of different nations and races.
The World Hunter Federation had to choose its commander at the base carefully, in case the chain of command broke down.
Team Leader Choi, an excellent adviser, recommended someone.
A man with extraordinary strength and a distinguished record as a Hunter, along with the strategy and knowledge to command a large army.
A Hunter and a soldier.
The only man to have reached the top of both professions.
Chuck Hagel—an S-rank Hunter active since the Great Cataclysm and the former Secretary of Defense of the good ol’ U.S. of A.
“Oh.
Sleeping Beauty finally showed up.
Or were you hibernating?”
Chuck Hagel’s idea of a greeting drew quiet laughter from the people lined up on either side of me.
It vanished without a trace the next moment.
“You’re laughing?
Does this fucked-up wartime situation look like a joke to you?”
“You lunatics.
From now on, anyone who laughs in front of me is getting their ass kicked, rank be damned.

I don’t care if you’re some pasty Yankee dumbass who thinks white skin is your greatest achievement in life, a darkie spouting bullshit about political correctness, or a yellow monkey who can’t stop staring at his smartphone.
I’ll beat every last one of you half to death.
Understood?”
“Yes, sir!”
“Goddamn it.
I can’t hear you!”
“Yes!!
Sir!!”
Only after everyone shouted at the top of their lungs did Chuck Hagel nod and take a drag from his cigar.
“Okay, ladies.”
Holy shit.
The man had presence.
He really was a living legend.
Even Senior Kim Soodan would have to concede he had a thing or two to learn from Hagel about taking over a stage.
Of course, those thick arms like a bear’s and the violence he was born with had a lot to do with creating this brisk atmosphere.
*He’s definitely the right man for the job.*
Just as I thought that, a military jeep came tearing across the runway and screeched to a stop in front of us.
A soldier in dress uniform hurriedly called out.
“Monster Wave!
We’ve received an emergency request for support.
It’s a Monster Wave!”
If I’d been an ordinary traveler, I would’ve taken a day to recover from jet lag.
But my life had parted ways with the word *ordinary* a long time ago, and there was no chance of them ever getting back together.
“Where is it?”

chapters.title: Chapter 793
paragraphs: With the whole world searching high and low, the chances that The Prophet had slipped into a major city full of people were close to zero.
So the tight search net spread across the Middle East, centered on the main force, was focused on monitoring underdeveloped areas. The place we headed to right away was no exception.
Wasteland stretched out on either side of a track so rough it hardly deserved to be called a road.
Beyond it lay a desert as vast as the open sea, dotted with little stands of trees like reefs.
And there, familiar faces were waiting for me.
“You’re with the main force, righ—huh?”
Surprise flashed across a face so young it belonged more to a boy than a man. Xiao Shen stared at me, dumbstruck, then cried out.
“Mr. Jin!”
“Damn it. Why does that Chinese kid have to be so loud?”
Chuck Hagel had come along in Team Leader Choi’s place in case anything happened. He let out a deep sigh.
“Do me a favor. Can’t you do something about that kid? Every time I see him, all he talks about is you. My ears are starting to hurt.”
“Well, he is pretty attached to me.”
“There’s attached, and then there’s that. Wilson wasn’t even that bad.”
“Who’s Wilson?”
“My dog. Whenever I came home after a few days away, he’d charge at me like a maniac. Must’ve thought I was an intruder.”
“Maybe Wilson just had a bad temper?”
“He died three years ago. It was summer.”
Shit. He’d played two cheat cards at once.
The Talullah moment and the summertime sentimentality hit me so hard I could barely breathe. By comparison, I was glad to see Xiao Shen, who’d just sprinted over like a track athlete.
“H-how could someone as shabby as Mr. Jin come all the way to a place this precious?”
“You’ve got that backward.”
“Oh.”
I patted the statue-like Xiao Shen on the shoulder, then looked around.
The place was definitely shabby.
Sticky blood and a foul stench covered everything.
As I gazed at a pool of blood the size of a small lake, a familiar voice reached me.
“You’re slow as hell. What took you so long?”
I turned. A figure was walking out of the darkness, countless pairs of monster eyes gleaming eerily behind him.
*Shing.*
Dozens of Hunters accompanying us as our supposed entourage reflexively drew their weapons. I stopped them with a casual wave and answered evenly.
“I got here as fast as I could.”
“Already talking nonsense. I’ve been waiting at least a week.”
“Well, I did sleep for a long time.”
“So you dumped this great king in a shithole like this while you rested without a care?”
“More or less.”
“Damn it.”
*Scuff. Scuff.*
For all his grumbling, he couldn’t hide the pleasure on his face as he drew closer.
I greeted the Skeleton King for the first time in a week.
“You’re still alive.”
“I am. Though I died a long time ago.”
They say even a dog can learn to recite poetry after three years at a village school.
I gave a quiet laugh at the Skeleton King’s practiced retort.
Behind him stood an army of well over a thousand monsters, even by a rough count.
Though, technically, it was an army of the undead.
“Looks like you’ve more or less finished up. What about the rest?”
“There are none. I took care of every last one.”
I nodded. If the Skeleton King said so, then that was that.

Even Michael Silbert, who’d kept his identity completely hidden by controlling the two energies coexisting inside him, had once aroused the Skeleton King’s suspicions. Whether he wanted the role or not, the Skeleton King was a monster—and when it came to magical power, he was the foremost expert.
*And his abilities are exceptional.*
In Murim, a Supreme Peak master is called a one-man army.
An S-rank Hunter in the modern world might not compare to a Supreme Peak master, of course, but they weren’t treated all that differently.
Each was a superhuman operating on a different level from ordinary people and Hunters.
Even among such people, the Skeleton King’s abilities stood out.
Any capable S-rank Hunter could take down an army of monsters alone. Finishing the job in less than thirty minutes without a single casualty was another matter.
“So that’s *i-mon-je-mon*—monsters against monsters.”
“*I-mon-je-mon*? What are you talking about?”
“You don’t know the four-character idiom? Passed down to us by our wise ancestors...”
“I have no need for it. I’m a citizen of the great United States of America.”
“If I remember right, just a few months ago you read ‘alligator’ as ‘arigatou.’”
“I’m Japanese American.”
“Konnichiwa.”
Is this guy fucking insane?

I stared at the Skeleton King, who could swap out his family tree at the drop of a hat, with some bemusement. But I didn’t have much to say. He’d held off a Monster Wave by himself. The least I could do was praise him instead of cursing him out.
I sighed and started to turn away. Then a question occurred to me.
*Why did he call for backup?*
The Skeleton King was powerful. As long as his magical power held out, he could create an endless army of the undead, and his own fighting ability was no joke.
So why?
Just to protect Xiao Shen?
Or...
*Was there something else?*
I turned back. Maybe my thoughts showed on my face, because the Skeleton King was watching me with a subdued look I hadn’t seen a moment ago.
“What?”
“Hmm.”
“What is it?”
After a brief silence, he answered.
“Even this great king doesn’t know.”
“What?”
“I couldn’t work out what did it, or how it was possible, no matter how much I thought about it. I tried to find it, but it had already vanished without a trace.”
“What do you mean, ‘it’? What the hell are you talking ab—”
“You’ll understand when you see it. You’ll remember, too.”
Remember what?
Before I could make sense of it, the Skeleton King gave an order.
“Bring them here.”
*Thud. Thud.*
At his gesture, three headless undead ogres approached with heavy steps. Then, with a care that seemed impossible for creatures their size, they set down what they were carrying.
The moment I saw the twenty bodies of people who had once been human, I understood what the Skeleton King meant.
“...Fuck.”
The curse escaped through my clenched teeth like a groan, mingling with the cool desert air.
Chuck Hagel came over to inspect the bodies. The cigar fell from his mouth.
“Holy shit.”
He wasn’t the only one.
“What the hell is this...?”
“Damn it. Henry?”
Shocked cries and curses broke out all around us. Those who made no sound simply stood there, stunned.
Was it because the bodies had been so horribly mutilated?
No.
The other Hunters and I had seen countless horrific sights. On a battlefield reeking of monsters and blood, even a severed limb wouldn’t make us bat an eye.
But even people like us had never seen anyone die like this before.
Almost none. A handful of us, myself included, had.
“Fuck. Jin, is this...?”
“Yes.”
I kept my voice as calm as I could.
Moonlight spilled through gaps in the slowly parting clouds. Beneath it lay twenty bodies drained of all vitality, their skin and bones shriveled like mummies.
I thought of someone who’d died the same way only a month ago, in an unnamed hideout.
“Siegfried Bassmann.”
One of humanity’s three great Grand Mages. Or rather, one of the three who *had* been.
Whatever had killed him was here in this desert.
*Ding!*
The distance to the site and back was the same, but the return trip felt incomparably shorter.
My head was full of questions.
*How?*
It wasn’t just me. Everyone had been certain Michael Silbert killed Siegfried Bassmann.
The reason was simple.

Bassmann was a Grand Mage, but unlike Magic Johnson, a War Mage who specialized in combat magic, he was a scholar through and through. That was why Johnson had suspected him of designing Area A. Bassmann was a master of barrier magic based on Magic Formations, as well as an expert on monsters.
Would a mage that skilled—and that reclusive—have protected his hideout with nothing but a tarp?
Like Area A, his hideout had been concealed behind all kinds of barriers. Only a handful of people in the world were strong enough to break through those spells.
And of that handful, Michael Silbert was the only one who’d wanted Bassmann dead.
But...
*We got it wrong.*
I knew it the moment I saw the bodies.
I’d been wrong. We all had.
At least on the day Siegfried Bassmann died, Michael Silbert hadn’t been the one to visit the Grand Mage’s hideout.
If Michael had killed him, the Quest window still occupying a corner of my vision should have disappeared long ago.

**System Quest An Unknown Death** The reclusive Grand Mage, Siegfried Bassmann, has died for unknown reasons. But everything has a cause. Discover how he died and who killed him. **Grade:** Supreme Peak **Restriction:** Jin Taekyung **Mission:** Discover the truth behind his death (Incomplete) **Reward:** ??? **Failure:** ???
The System wasn’t all-powerful.
It gave me a vague direction to follow, but it never told me how far I was from my destination or what traps lay along the way.
That was probably why I hadn’t noticed anything strange about this Quest, even when I checked my System messages and Quest windows right after waking up.
I’d simply assumed it was still open because I hadn’t gotten the full truth about Bassmann’s death out of Michael Silbert.
To me, the Cataclysm Main Quest was the root I had to pull out right away. Everything else was just a branch.
That had been my crucial mistake.

Branches and roots served different purposes, but they were parts of the same tree. Follow a root upward and you reached a branch. Trace a branch down and you reached the root hidden deep underground.
I just hadn’t uncovered it yet. Even if it was hidden now, I could find it someday.
And in that sense, the first person I went to see after returning to the main force was one of the largest branches on the sick tree that was Michael Silbert.
“Someone died about two hours ago. Not just one person—twenty.”
A faint smile crossed the gaunt face on the other side of the table as soon as I sat down and said it.
“You’re impatient. You’ve invited a guest here—can’t he at least have a cup of coffee?”
Coffee. A smile. A guest.
I licked my parched lips.
Strangely, I wasn’t angry. No—maybe I’d reached the limit of my patience the moment we began.
“I’m going to ask you one thing. Listen carefully and answer me, you crow bastard.”
Huginn froze under my killing intent. I put into words the question that hadn’t left my mind the entire way back.
“Did The Prophet kill Siegfried Bassmann?”

chapters.title: Chapter 794
paragraphs: “Did The Prophet kill Siegfried Bassmann?”
Huginn clamped his mouth shut at the killing intent in my voice. Just as he had for the past week. Just as he would forever, it seemed.
But unlike the investigators who’d interrogated him so far, I had no intention of backing down.
No matter what it took.
“What do you think of this room? Nice atmosphere, don’t you think?”
At my sudden question, Huginn’s eyebrow twitched.
I stood and slowly paced around the spacious room, furnished with nothing but a table and chairs.

“No cameras running twenty-four hours a day, no observation window. Must feel like paradise to a prisoner, right? I went through something similar once, so I know how awful it feels to be watched every second.”
“That’s why I brought you here. I thought it’d be more convenient for both of us. Like I said, no prying eyes, and...”
I dropped back into my seat with a thump. “The soundproofing magic is perfect, too.”
He didn’t answer, but I knew.
The look in his sunken eyes told me he’d understood exactly what I meant.
After a brief silence, a snicker slipped between Huginn’s lips.
*Pfft.*
The breathy sound grew louder until his laughter rang through the room. His shoulders shook for a long while before he finally spoke.
“Is that all?”
“What?”
“I asked if that’s all you’ve got. Torture, threats—whatever you’re going to do, do it properly. That isn’t even worth laughing at.”
This time it was my turn to keep my mouth shut. Huginn took the baton, his face full of scorn.
“You won’t get the answer you want from me, no matter what you try. Just like those bastards who came before you.”
*Those bastards who came before me.*
So that was why he’d grown so gaunt since I last saw him. Apparently, I wasn’t the first visitor.
Of course, I’d more or less guessed as much.
A bunch of countries could join forces, form the UN, and draft an international convention against torture. In the end, if no one found out, what did it matter?
And Huginn had been Michael Silbert’s right hand, handling missions both big and small.

A traitor to humanity who held a vital secret had locked his lips tight. The American torturers seasoned in the Middle East had probably put their skills to work while the leadership looked the other way.
*And every one of them failed.*
I studied Huginn after his outburst.
His mana was suppressed and his entire body bound, but he was still an S-rank Hunter. More than that, he was an exceptional fighter chosen to be Michael Silbert’s right hand.
Even torture and mental magic would struggle to break his will.
“Just talk and it’ll all be over. Like the others who were captured with you, all you have to do is tell the truth.”
“Go fuck yourself.”
“Michael Silbert left you a final message, didn’t he? You’ve heard it by now.”
“I have. But this is entirely my choice. Ever since I was five—”
“Shut up. I don’t want to hear it. I don’t care if you were a piano prodigy at five or an orphan who grew to hate the world.”
Everyone had their sob story.
But I wasn’t some late-night radio host, and I had no reason to listen to a villain’s tired old backstory.
I did know what he wanted most right now, though.
“If you tell the truth, I’ll promise you one thing.”
“A promise?”
“Yeah. A promise.”
“Then you won’t get an answer. I don’t need any—”
I cut off his scornful reply with the one line I’d prepared.
“I’ll kill you.”
“As painlessly as possible. Cleanly. I can’t promise to let you go—I couldn’t keep that promise. But I can do this today.”
“You bastard...”
“Don’t deny it. You’d rather die than keep living like this, wouldn’t you?”
He tried to hide it, but I could see it.
Resignation and spite mingled in his eyes as they began to waver. His tongue, though, still refused to swallow his pride.
“Cut the bullshit. There’s no way you can make me talk.”
“From what you’ve been saying, you definitely know something.”
“By the way, how old are you now? Around fifty, if I remember right... Still young. You’ve got a long life ahead of you.”
In Murim, fifty was old enough to be called a grandfather without anyone batting an eye. But in the modern world, fifty was still the prime of life.
Plenty of people with money lived past a hundred thanks to cutting-edge medicine and magical health care.
And Huginn was an S-rank Hunter. Even with his mana suppressed, his vitality was on a completely different level from an ordinary person’s.
“Our crow friend’s going to live a long time. Of course, he’ll spend the rest of it in prison.”
I leaned my chair way back and gazed at the pure white ceiling, my voice calm as I went on.

“A sealed room without a ray of sunlight. Someone watching you around the clock. Interrogations whenever they feel like it. Or should I say torture? After everything you’ve done, they’ll probably be pretty brutal for a long time.”

“You’ve been tough enough to make it this far, somehow... But what happens when it goes on for fifty years? Well, at least you’ll stay healthy. They’ll shower you with potions after every round of cutting.”
Millions had been killed or injured in the terrorist attacks.
In front of a humanity consumed by grief and rage, the word *human rights* had already become meaningless.
If an article appeared in the *New York Times* tomorrow morning saying Huginn had been tortured, people all over the world would be shocked—and start collecting donations.
Not for his legal fees. For potions to prolong his suffering forever.
And as time crawled by, Huginn’s mind would slowly fall apart.
Or maybe it had already begun to crack.
“Team Leader Choi told me something interesting on the way here. Apparently, you caused a bit of a commotion on the plane. Are you sick? Or was it a seizure?”
Probably the latter.
Pain was the same for everyone, even an S-rank Hunter with a strong body and mind. He just knew how to endure it.
Getting used to pain didn’t make it hurt less.
“Why aren’t you answering? You’re making me feel awkward for asking. If you’re already like this, how are you going to get through the rest of your life?”
Just as I straightened from my half-reclined position, a wet crunch sounded and blood poured from Huginn’s mouth.
He’d bitten his tongue.
“Ouch. That must hurt.”
I clicked my tongue, pulled a potion from my Inventory, and shoved it into Huginn’s mouth. The bleeding stopped almost at once, and his half-severed tongue healed.
“Let’s not make this harder on each other. I didn’t remove your gag so you could bite your tongue. Besides, I’m starting to run out of the potions I brought...”
*Crunch. Splurt.*
The moment I said I was running out, Huginn bit his tongue again. I sighed.
“I told you not to do that.”
Then I rummaged through my Inventory and took out a potion.
Or rather, a box packed full of them.
*Thud.*
“Please. I’m asking nicely. I’ve only got about three hundred left. Okay?”
“At least this time you only cut off a little bit of your tongue.”
“Open your mouth. Come on. Say ‘ah.’”
Huginn stared at me blankly instead of answering, so I slapped him across the face.
*Smack!*
Teeth flew in every direction.
But I wasn’t satisfied with stopping there.
*Smack! Crunch.*
His jaw joint broke, and his mouth fell open on its own.
“That’s it. Good job. You listen so well. But you’ve got tartar buildup. When was your last cleaning?”
Blood smeared around his mouth, Huginn stammered out an answer.
“Tw-two years ago...”
“That’s a while. Potions aren’t a cure-all. Tartar isn’t an injury, so they won’t heal it. You need to brush your teeth. Or go to the dentist. What do you need to do?”
“Brush my teeth, go to the dentist...”

“What are you talking about, dumbass? Just use Clean magic. Is your head for decoration? Have you kept it around since birth so you can use it as a weapon in an emergency? Did you dream of becoming a Dullahan in elementary school?”
“Why are you even—”

“But you little shit. I’ve let you get away with enough. You fucking bastard, you keep dragging this out like you’re the last royal chef of Joseon, carefully tasting everything first. What is this, a royal banquet? You’re not leaving until you’ve used every potion in this box.”
“I’ll tell you! I’ll tell you everything—!”
“Shut up.”
I didn’t know what I was saying. Or why I was acting like this.
All I knew was that the heat that had been creeping up from my gut finally reached my head.
*Grab. Wham!*
I snatched up a potion bottle and swung it at the top of his head. At the dull impact and surge of pain, his tightly bound body trembled.
“W-wait!”
“This is reinforced glass, you bastard.”
*Wham! Wham! Crash!*
Even reinforced glass could only take about three hits.
Shards showered over the top of his head, now spurting blood. The potion inside poured down with them.
*Splash.*
Healing and pain at the same time. A miracle.
But before he’d finished healing, I grabbed another bottle.
*Whack! Whack! Whaaack!*
*Crash!*
When I came to my senses, I found myself pawing at an empty box.
“Is... is it over?”
“No.”
I pulled a fresh box from my Inventory.
“Hang in there. There are still two hundred left.”
“You can do it. Let’s keep at it together. I can do this all day. I might even be fine doing it every day from now on.”
Huginn stared at me wide-eyed, then spoke in a trembling voice.
“I-I said I’d talk. Why are you...”
“Bullshit. When?”
“I’ve been saying it for ages. Over and over. The whole time...”
“What a ridiculous bastard. Do I look like an idiot to you?”
“I’m telling the truth! I really did!”
“Are you yelling at me right now? Do you—do you feel so wronged you can’t stand it?”
“N-no, that’s not what I—”
“Forget it. You hurt my feelings. I’ve already got this box out, so let’s finish it before we talk again.”
I thought I might have vaguely heard him say something like that, but what did it matter?
Thanks to Huginn’s excellent teamwork, we emptied the second box of potions, too. When I took out a third, I heard his tearful voice.
“Stop! Stooop!”
The mouth even veteran torturers hadn’t been able to pry open was now running free.
Maybe the genuine madness I’d shown had moved him, I thought. I closed the box I’d opened halfway.
“You finally understand how sincere I am.”
“...The promise you made earlier?”
“I’ll keep it. If you want to die that badly.”
“How can I trust you?”
“That’s up to you. But I swear on everything I have. That’s all.”
“So? Your answer?”
Huginn swallowed, then finally spoke.
“He did.”
“Be precise. Again.”
“The one who killed Siegfried Bassmann... was the person they call The Prophet.”
There was no doubt. Huginn was telling the truth.
But just as my suspicion became certainty, another question came to mind.
“The person they call The Prophet?”
Maybe it was because his mind was foggy. He looked like he’d said something he didn’t need to, but it was too late to take back words once he’d let them out.
*There’s more.*
I’d thought Michael Silbert and The Prophet were connected, but I hadn’t been able to pin down exactly how.
I glared at him, my eyes sinking deep, and spoke.
“Tell me what you mean. Tell me everything you know about The Prophet.”
“T-that...”
It was ironic.
He had to struggle not to live, but to die. Yet Huginn had been driven to the edge of a cliff. He had no choices left.
“He’s Muninn.”
“What?”
The moment I blurted out the question, a memory flashed through my mind: the day Huginn first came to Ares Guild.
Two ravens engraved into a corner of his business card.
And... the conversation I’d had with Team Leader Choi.
“Huginn and Muninn. Those two ravens are symbols of a certain god from Norse mythology.”
“Who?”
“Odin.”
I blinked.
Odin, the supreme god. And the two ravens who served him: Huginn and Muninn.
There had never been just one crow to begin with.

“Go fuck yourself.”

Everyone had their sob story.

A promise.”

His tongue, though, still refused to swallow his pride.

There’s no way you can make me talk.”
“From what you’ve been saying, you definitely know something.”
“By the way, how old are you now?

You’ve got a long life ahead of you.”
In Murim, fifty was old enough to be called a grandfather without anyone batting an eye.
But in the modern world, fifty was still the prime of life.
Plenty of people with money lived past a hundred thanks to cutting-edge medicine and magical health care.
And Huginn was an S-rank Hunter.
Even with his mana suppressed, his vitality was on a completely different level from an ordinary person’s.
“Our crow friend’s going to live a long time.
Of course, he’ll spend the rest of it in prison.”

Or should I say torture?

Millions had been killed or injured in the terrorist attacks.

*Ding. Ding. Ding.*
The System messages appearing before my eyes and ringing in my ears were the final confirmation that everything Huginn had said was true.
But a Quest was just a Quest. I wanted more.
Everything about Muninn—or the person called The Prophet.
“Spill everything you know about him. Don’t leave out a single thing.”
I leaned in until Huginn’s trembling breath brushed my face.
“This isn’t what we agreed at the start...”
“An agreement? Of course I’ll keep it. Just not now.”
The condition for keeping my promise in the first place was confirming that The Prophet had killed Siegfried Bassmann. But in this relationship, I was the one holding all the cards.
“Talk. Or you’ll rot in prison until the day you die.”
“You know what I’m like. If I say I’ll do something, I do it. Quit trying to outthink me and open your mouth. Go ahead and mix in a lie if you think you can get away with it.”
You could learn a lot from a person’s eyes. The resignation that had just taken over Huginn’s told me he’d finally given up.
“...Fuck.”
The curse came out almost like a sigh. Then he began to speak.
“I don’t know much about him, either. Not exactly what the current Muninn is like.”
I’d grabbed a potion bottle at his first words, but what he hurriedly added made me frown.
*The current Muninn?*
That was too loaded a phrase to brush off.
It sounded as if...
“Like he hasn’t always been the same person.”
“That’s right. He’s changed several times.”
My mind raced. I slowly set down the potion bottle and stared at Huginn.
“Tell me more.”
“Since I became an adult and officially began serving the Guild Master, I’ve met three Muninns. Including the ones before then, the person now called The Prophet is the fifth Muninn.”
“Before that?”
“Before the Great Cataclysm ended. There were war orphans everywhere you went. I was one of them, though I wasn’t a little kid.”
I didn’t need the details to picture what had happened.
Good people and bad people saw the world differently. Good people might have pitied the countless orphans left by the Great Cataclysm. Others saw a way to further their ambitions.
*Lee Jungryong found Go Jun the same way.*
The good fortune of Awakening came equally to everyone in humanity after their twentieth birthday.
In that sense, orphans with no one to rely on were lottery tickets that hadn’t been scratched yet. Huginn must have been a diamond Michael Silbert had plucked from the mud.
And...
“That’s when you met Muninn.”
“More precisely, the first Muninn. That was the first and last time I saw him.”
“The last? What happened after that?”

“The Great Cataclysm ended. The Guild Master wanted to keep my existence secret, so after I’d trained in secret for a while, he brought me to his side. That was the day I became Huginn. He introduced me to a man I’d never seen before.”
“The new Muninn?”
Huginn nodded.
“What happened to the first Muninn?”
“I don’t know. The Guild Master only told me he’d gone missing during the Great Cataclysm. He probably died in the war.”
“Gone missing? If he was Michael Silbert’s right-hand man, he must have been highly skilled.”
Huginn gave a bitter smile at my look.
“If you don’t believe me, I can’t help that. But it’s all I know. I hadn’t even Awakened back then. I wasn’t Huginn yet.”
“When exactly was this?”
“Spring of 2021. The Guild Master was already famous. After the Great Battle of Paris, he was becoming one of the heroes who represented France—no, Europe.”
I studied Huginn’s expression for a moment, but couldn’t find any sign of a lie in his face or eyes.
The important part came next.
“The Prophet... Who’s the fifth Muninn?”
“Hmm.”
“Think back. Just tell me what you know. Everything you saw and heard.”
Huginn frowned in thought, but it didn’t take him long to answer.
“A white man. Most of his face was covered, so I didn’t get a good look at him. His build didn’t seem suited to close combat, though. That was only my impression.”
You couldn’t judge a Hunter by their build alone—not when you had someone like Jeok Cheongang, with his slight frame, as proof.
But if someone as skilled as Huginn had gotten that impression, it was worth taking seriously.
The problem was that it gave me nowhere near enough to identify The Prophet.
“A white man. Possibly a ranged Hunter. That’s all you know?”
Huginn swallowed dryly at my calm but icy voice, then answered.
“That’s why I said I didn’t know much. I saw him only once, about three years ago. And even then, the Guild Master ordered me to leave right away.”
“Then how do you know he’s The Prophet? Or that he killed Siegfried Bassmann?”
“The Guild Master told me when the time came. That’s how it’s always worked with Muninn.”
“Always?”

“I stayed by the Guild Master’s side and acted as his hands and feet. They were weapons he sent on more dangerous missions. They’d be gone for a year, sometimes several years, then suddenly appear again. I was always brought in afterward.”
“For example?”
“Information about Sky—Cheon Taemin. And...”
“And what?”
“That...”
*Smack!*
My palm whipped across Huginn’s cheek. He spat blood and muttered a few words through his pained expression.
“Tokyo. Leviathan. A Magic Gem.”
“The Muninn from three years ago brought back all that information. That’s everything. Damn it.”
I stared at Huginn, frozen like a statue.
Anger?
No. Shock.
*He knew about Leviathan from the start. He used a Magic Gem to lure it to Tokyo.*
And the one who gave that information to Michael Silbert was none other than Muninn—the very man now called The Prophet.
The truth sent a chill down my spine, as if someone had poured ice water over me.
*How the hell?*
For all the heights modern civilization had reached, the deep sea remained largely unexplored. Yet he’d learned of the calamity lurking in its dark depths.
Perhaps he’d done it all on Michael Silbert’s orders. But was that the whole story?
*Damn it.*
I swallowed the curse rising in my chest.
Now I understood why no one had ever noticed Muninn.

A hidden blade who visited Michael Silbert in secret, sometimes after a year, more often after several. Unlike Huginn, he hadn’t stayed at Silbert’s side day to day. And since he was sometimes replaced because of his dangerous missions, there’d been no way to notice him.
Even Huginn, who’d handled most of Michael Silbert’s affairs as his right hand, barely knew anything about Muninn.
One thing was certain.
*He’s dangerous. Far more dangerous than I thought.*
He’d taken down Siegfried Bassmann, an outstanding Grand Mage, all on his own. He’d also drawn the outlines of the events behind this terrorist attack and supplied the information to Michael Silbert.
*Michael Silbert hadn’t done it on his own.*
Michael Silbert had reached his current position thanks to the loyal Muninns who’d died for him.
I didn’t know what the earlier Muninns had accomplished. But the man I now knew as The Prophet was far more than a mere subordinate.
Another root. Or a second Michael Silbert.
*Where the hell did he find people like them?*
No matter how vast the world was, no matter how many secrets it held, things eventually leaked out somewhere. Just as the great Guilds secretly trained new S-rank Hunters beyond the public eye.
This was beyond anything I’d imagined.
*They must have been handling the dirty work for a long time.*
Five Muninns. And the fifth Muninn.

They were Michael Silbert’s darkest shadows. For years, they’d smuggled unrefined Magic Gems out of the Middle East and Africa without pause and stored them away. They’d been his warehouse keepers, his informants, and the blades he used to eliminate rivals.
At least until Michael Silbert died.
*But now the Prophet had all of it.*
He wasn’t merely a pair of hands and feet like Huginn. The arm called Muninn had broken away from its dead master’s body and grown a body of its own.
The Prophet.
An heir who commanded countless fanatics of a religion followed by twenty percent of the world’s population, and who’d inherited everything his dead master had hidden.
That madman now held the knife by the handle.
And maybe...
“Fuck.”
No. Not that. I couldn’t jump to conclusions on information I wasn’t even sure of, especially now.
I forced the thought from my mind and sprang to my feet.

I had to tell everyone what I’d learned and call back the search teams scattered across the Middle East, as fast as I could. The Prophet was strong enough to kill a Grand Mage alone. I’d sent those teams into the desert to prevent more deaths, not to throw their lives away.
“W-wait!”
Right. Huginn was still here.
I turned at his desperate cry. Before he could say another word, I snatched a potion bottle from the box and brought it down on the crown of his head with lightning speed.
*Crash! Thud.*
Huginn lost consciousness in a single blow and toppled over with his chair.
A concussion at the very least. But he’d been drenched in potion, so he’d probably be fine.
“Live a nice, long life, okay?”
I spat phlegm toward him, brushed the glass dust off my hand, and walked outside.
I nodded toward the torture technicians pacing outside the door.
“He talked a fair bit, but there might be more he hasn’t told us.”
“Oh, then...?”
“Get it out of him. Squeeze out every last thing, even if you have to wring his soul dry.”
Their faces lit up.
“Yes, sir.”
“I’ll do my best. There are a lot of methods we haven’t tried yet.”
“Oh, look at this, Michael! Santa left us a whole box of potions!”
“We’ll put them to good use, Boss!”
A promise?
You make those with people. Not trash like Huginn.
“Everyone on the leadership team, to the strategy room. Right now.”
I listened to Team Leader Choi answer over the phone as I crossed the hallway. Then I turned to look out the window.
Tonight, the moon showing through the clouds looked unusually red.

Ding.
Ding.*
The System messages appearing before my eyes and ringing in my ears were the final confirmation that everything Huginn had said was true.
But a Quest was just a Quest.
I wanted more.
Everything about Muninn—or the person called The Prophet.
“Spill everything you know about him.
Don’t leave out a single thing.”
I leaned in until Huginn’s trembling breath brushed my face.
“This isn’t what we agreed at the start...”
“An agreement?
Of course I’ll keep it.
Just not now.”
The condition for keeping my promise in the first place was confirming that The Prophet had killed Siegfried Bassmann.
But in this relationship, I was the one holding all the cards.
“Talk.
Or you’ll rot in prison until the day you die.”
“You know what I’m like.
If I say I’ll do something, I do it.
Quit trying to outthink me and open your mouth.
Go ahead and mix in a lie if you think you can get away with it.”
You could learn a lot from a person’s eyes.
The resignation that had just taken over Huginn’s told me he’d finally given up.
“...Fuck.”
The curse came out almost like a sigh.
Then he began to speak.
“I don’t know much about him, either.
Not exactly what the current Muninn is like.”
I’d grabbed a potion bottle at his first words, but what he hurriedly added made me frown.
*The current Muninn?*
That was too loaded a phrase to brush off.
It sounded as if...
“Like he hasn’t always been the same person.”
“That’s right.
He’s changed several times.”
My mind raced.
I slowly set down the potion bottle and stared at Huginn.
“Tell me more.”
“Since I became an adult and officially began serving the Guild Master, I’ve met three Muninns.
Including the ones before then, the person now called The Prophet is the fifth Muninn.”
“Before that?”
“Before the Great Cataclysm ended.
There were war orphans everywhere you went.
I was one of them, though I wasn’t a little kid.”
I didn’t need the details to picture what had happened.
Good people and bad people saw the world differently.
Good people might have pitied the countless orphans left by the Great Cataclysm.
Others saw a way to further their ambitions.
*Lee Jungryong found Go Jun the same way.*
The good fortune of Awakening came equally to everyone in humanity after their twentieth birthday.
In that sense, orphans with no one to rely on were lottery tickets that hadn’t been scratched yet.
Huginn must have been a diamond Michael Silbert had plucked from the mud.
And...
“That’s when you met Muninn.”
“More precisely, the first Muninn.
That was the first and last time I saw him.”
“The last?
What happened after that?”
“The Great Cataclysm ended.
The Guild Master wanted to keep my existence secret, so after I’d trained in secret for a while, he brought me to his side.
That was the day I became Huginn.
He introduced me to a man I’d never seen before.”
“The new Muninn?”
Huginn nodded.
“What happened to the first Muninn?”
“I don’t know.
The Guild Master only told me he’d gone missing during the Great Cataclysm.
He probably died in the war.”
“Gone missing?
If he was Michael Silbert’s right-hand man, he must have been highly skilled.”
Huginn gave a bitter smile at my look.
“If you don’t believe me, I can’t help that.
But it’s all I know.
I hadn’t even Awakened back then.
I wasn’t Huginn yet.”
“When exactly was this?”
“Spring of 2021.
The Guild Master was already famous.
After the Great Battle of Paris, he was becoming one of the heroes who represented France—no, Europe.”
I studied Huginn’s expression for a moment, but couldn’t find any sign of a lie in his face or eyes.
The important part came next.
“The Prophet...
Who’s the fifth Muninn?”
“Hmm.”
“Think back.
Just tell me what you know.
Everything you saw and heard.”
Huginn frowned in thought, but it didn’t take him long to answer.
“A white man.
Most of his face was covered, so I didn’t get a good look at him.
His build didn’t seem suited to close combat, though.
That was only my impression.”
You couldn’t judge a Hunter by their build alone—not when you had someone like Jeok Cheongang, with his slight frame, as proof.
But if someone as skilled as Huginn had gotten that impression, it was worth taking seriously.
The problem was that it gave me nowhere near enough to identify The Prophet.
“A white man.
Possibly a ranged Hunter.
That’s all you know?”
Huginn swallowed dryly at my calm but icy voice, then answered.
“That’s why I said I didn’t know much.
I saw him only once, about three years ago.
And even then, the Guild Master ordered me to leave right away.”
“Then how do you know he’s The Prophet?
Or that he killed Siegfried Bassmann?”
“The Guild Master told me when the time came.
That’s how it’s always worked with Muninn.”
“Always?”
“I stayed by the Guild Master’s side and acted as his hands and feet.
They were weapons he sent on more dangerous missions.
They’d be gone for a year, sometimes several years, then suddenly appear again.
I was always brought in afterward.”
“For example?”
“Information about Sky—Cheon Taemin.
And...”
“And what?”
“That...”
*Smack!*
My palm whipped across Huginn’s cheek.
He spat blood and muttered a few words through his pained expression.
“Tokyo.
Leviathan.
A Magic Gem.”
“The Muninn from three years ago brought back all that information.
That’s everything.
Damn it.”
I stared at Huginn, frozen like a statue.
Anger?
No.
Shock.
*He knew about Leviathan from the start.
He used a Magic Gem to lure it to Tokyo.*
And the one who gave that information to Michael Silbert was none other than Muninn—the very man now called The Prophet.
The truth sent a chill down my spine, as if someone had poured ice water over me.
*How the hell?*
For all the heights modern civilization had reached, the deep sea remained largely unexplored.
Yet he’d learned of the calamity lurking in its dark depths.
Perhaps he’d done it all on Michael Silbert’s orders.
But was that the whole story?
*Damn it.*
I swallowed the curse rising in my chest.
Now I understood why no one had ever noticed Muninn.
A hidden blade who visited Michael Silbert in secret, sometimes after a year, more often after several.
Unlike Huginn, he hadn’t stayed at Silbert’s side day to day.
And since he was sometimes replaced because of his dangerous missions, there’d been no way to notice him.
Even Huginn, who’d handled most of Michael Silbert’s affairs as his right hand, barely knew anything about Muninn.
One thing was certain.
*He’s dangerous.
Far more dangerous than I thought.*
He’d taken down Siegfried Bassmann, an outstanding Grand Mage, all on his own.
He’d also drawn the outlines of the events behind this terrorist attack and supplied the information to Michael Silbert.
*Michael Silbert hadn’t done it on his own.*
Michael Silbert had reached his current position thanks to the loyal Muninns who’d died for him.
I didn’t know what the earlier Muninns had accomplished.
But the man I now knew as The Prophet was far more than a mere subordinate.
Another root.
Or a second Michael Silbert.
*Where the hell did he find people like them?*
No matter how vast the world was, no matter how many secrets it held, things eventually leaked out somewhere.
Just as the great Guilds secretly trained new S-rank Hunters beyond the public eye.
This was beyond anything I’d imagined.
*They must have been handling the dirty work for a long time.*
Five Muninns.
And the fifth Muninn.
They were Michael Silbert’s darkest shadows.
For years, they’d smuggled unrefined Magic Gems out of the Middle East and Africa without pause and stored them away.
They’d been his warehouse keepers, his informants, and the blades he used to eliminate rivals.
At least until Michael Silbert died.
*But now the Prophet had all of it.*
He wasn’t merely a pair of hands and feet like Huginn.
The arm called Muninn had broken away from its dead master’s body and grown a body of its own.
The Prophet.
An heir who commanded countless fanatics of a religion followed by twenty percent of the world’s population, and who’d inherited everything his dead master had hidden.
That madman now held the knife by the handle.
And maybe...
“Fuck.”
No.
Not that.
I couldn’t jump to conclusions on information I wasn’t even sure of, especially now.
I forced the thought from my mind and sprang to my feet.
I had to tell everyone what I’d learned and call back the search teams scattered across the Middle East, as fast as I could.
The Prophet was strong enough to kill a Grand Mage alone.
I’d sent those teams into the desert to prevent more deaths, not to throw their lives away.
“W-wait!”
Right.
Huginn was still here.
I turned at his desperate cry.
Before he could say another word, I snatched a potion bottle from the box and brought it down on the crown of his head with lightning speed.
*Crash!
Thud.*
Huginn lost consciousness in a single blow and toppled over with his chair.
A concussion at the very least.
But he’d been drenched in potion, so he’d probably be fine.
“Live a nice, long life, okay?”
I spat phlegm toward him, brushed the glass dust off my hand, and walked outside.
I nodded toward the torture technicians pacing outside the door.
“He talked a fair bit, but there might be more he hasn’t told us.”
“Oh, then...?”
“Get it out of him.
Squeeze out every last thing, even if you have to wring his soul dry.”
Their faces lit up.
“Yes, sir.”
“I’ll do my best.
There are a lot of methods we haven’t tried yet.”
“Oh, look at this, Michael!
Santa left us a whole box of potions!”
“We’ll put them to good use, Boss!”
A promise?
You make those with people.
Not trash like Huginn.
“Everyone on the leadership team, to the strategy room.
Right now.”
I listened to Team Leader Choi answer over the phone as I crossed the hallway.
Then I turned to look out the window.
Tonight, the moon showing through the clouds looked unusually red.

chapters.title: Chapter 796
paragraphs: That night, someone stopped in the middle of a hurried walk to look out the window. The moon seemed redder than usual.
They weren’t imagining it.
A blood moon.

The phenomenon sometimes occurred during a total lunar eclipse or when the atmosphere was unstable. With magical power levels rising day by day, not just the atmosphere but the climate itself was changing.
*Whoosh.*
The scattered raindrops grew heavier.
A downpour that seemed out of place in this barren land, where the annual rainfall was less than 250 millimeters, soon blanketed the whole area.
Across the endless sand and the few trees scattered through it.
And over the head of someone invisible to the naked eye.
*Tap. Patter-patter.*
The rain struck an unseen barrier and bounced away without touching him.
The Prophet, crossing the vast desert behind an invisible barrier, abruptly looked up at the sky.
The sky was dark and noisy. Storm clouds that had looked ominous for days were unleashing rain and thunder with furious force, as though enraged by what had happened on this land.
The Prophet paid them no mind. He studied the sky—or rather, opened his senses wide and listened to every sound around him.
*Rumble. Rrrumble.*
Thunder boomed ceaselessly overhead. The Prophet paused to focus on the sounds around him, then muttered,
“They’re gone.”
The sharp cries of eagles that had echoed in the distance were gone.
The persistent flying beasts some pursuer must have sent after him had finally given up and turned back.
*They were a nuisance. Good riddance.*

Avoiding satellite surveillance and unmanned reconnaissance aircraft was easy enough. Magical power mixed into the atmosphere shielded him from tracking, and concealment spells weren’t meant for making stew.
But those eagles were different. Even the Familiars kept by the few mages who specialized in mental magic were dirt under their claws by comparison.
They’d followed him for hundreds of kilometers without slowing down. And their eyes shone so brightly with magical power that he’d almost thought they could see through his spells.
*They can’t be Familiars... It must be him.*
The Skeleton King. Or the Stone King.
The Prophet frowned without realizing it. A mere monster, siding with humans.
The desert was still vast, but the undead army under that creature’s command would cover more ground and cut the search time drastically.
*I didn’t expect this.*

Then again, more than one thing had defied his expectations. He hadn’t thought Michael Silbert would fall so easily, or that the World Hunter Federation would bring its chaotic ranks under control so quickly and close in on him.
But The Prophet knew what all those surprises had in common. One man.
*Jin Taekyung.*
Others had shone brightly before, but they’d all been meteors: a brief flash, then gone in the blink of an eye.
Jin Taekyung was different. He was a comet.
From the moment he appeared, he’d been part of the celestial body that was the world. Now he’d become its center.
He was growing so quickly that no one could predict his limits. So quickly that all The Prophet’s preparations threatened to come to nothing.
*Clink.*
His fingers strayed to something, drawing out a faint metallic sound.
Forcing down the impatience welling up inside him, The Prophet murmured,
“Just a little more. Just a little more, and it’ll be complete.”
Time was the problem.
He still hadn’t gathered everything needed for a plan that could not tolerate the slightest error, and his enemies’ net was tightening fast.
That left The Prophet only one option.
*Hunt.*
But time was short. To complete his plan successfully, he had to make it bigger and bolder than before.
For example...
*Vroom.*
From atop a high sand dune, he spotted transport vehicles moving through a thick cloud of dust. His eyes lit up.
“Chikushō.”
At Yamamoto Genji’s low curse, the Self-Defense Forces Hunters edged away from Japan’s S-rank Hunter and exchanged glances.
Japan was hardly a Hunter powerhouse, but every Hunter it had dispatched to the Middle East was a veteran among veterans. They’d known one another for years, too. By now, a glance was enough.
*What’s his problem?*
*Isn’t it obvious? Who else could it be?*
*Eeh? Jin-sama?*
*Yeah. That transmission from headquarters really set Yamamoto-san off.*
The story was simple. About thirty minutes earlier, headquarters had ordered an emergency withdrawal. Yamamoto Genji had refused.
A reply had come at once—not in the communications officer’s stiff voice, but in a young man’s unmistakable one.
“When Leviathan was wrecking Tokyo Bay, you didn’t come even when we called, you son of a bitch. What? You’re not coming now? Give me your coordinates. If you won’t come to me, I’ll come to you.”
Who was Jin Taekyung?
The only person who could fill the void left by the unconscious Cheon Taemin. The Alliance Leader of the World Hunter Federation, with the support of all humanity.
But people shouldn’t forget his temper, either. Sometimes—no, fairly often—he acted without a thought for the consequences. And he had the strength to back it up.

The Self-Defense Forces Hunters, their knees weak at the Supreme One’s reply—practically a murder threat—had desperately tried to talk Yamamoto down. Even after climbing into an evacuation vehicle, Yamamoto Genji still couldn’t contain his anger.
“Konoyarō. How dare a Chōsenjin...!”
The others pretended not to hear. At a time like this, they needed to be blind and deaf.
They didn’t much like Yamamoto’s attitude themselves. But if word reached their superiors, they’d get cursed out—and Japan would get dragged into it with them.
*More bad press?*
*No. Absolutely not.*

The Defense Minister, who had played a major role in the Leviathan incident—including preparing a kamikaze operation—was now in a federal prison after his connection to Michael Silbert had come to light. And the kind but stupid Prime Minister couldn’t even go a few days without spewing more shit.

[Japanese Prime Minister Koizumi: “People of Yamato, fight for Jin-sama, the great shogun who defeated Susanoo for us!”] [Asked about the strategy for the Self-Defense Forces’ upcoming deployment to the Middle East, Prime Minister Koizumi said, “Combat should be fun, cool, and sexy.”] [Former U.S. President Joseph Biden: “I understand the Japanese Prime Minister. In the early stages of my dementia, I didn’t know what I was saying, either.”] [Chuck Hagel: “I think they’re both just crazy.”]
The Self-Defense Forces Hunters felt sorry for themselves.

The Defense Minister was set to spend his twilight years in federal prison, while the Prime Minister was using the media as a loudspeaker to announce, without a hint of restraint, that Japan’s leader was a lunatic.
Even Korean netizens, who’d been holding back because of the tense mood, had started saying things like this:

└ **Top comment:** I don’t really want to bring this up when things are already tense, but... do those guys have something against Japan? └ The Japanese Prime Minister and Defense Minister are anti-Japan, lmao. Fuck. └ If you ask me, they must’ve had something going on in a past life. └ One of them was a turtle ship in a past life, and the other was a lunchbox bomb. Seriously, it’s not easy to spew that much shit. └ I wonder if this is how the independence fighters felt when they saw Mutaguchi Renya... └ Shadow independence army. Agreed. └ Sushi country: “Uh, what are those guys doing?”

And now Yamamoto Genji, once called the pride of the island nation, had lost face too. People had learned that he’d failed to show up twice in a row: first during the Leviathan incident, then at the launch ceremony.
Why had he skipped the launch ceremony?
The Self-Defense Forces Hunters didn’t know. If they’d known the real reason, they’d have spat in his face, pride of the island nation or not.
Yamamoto Genji had simply been... embarrassed.
*Damn it. I should’ve gone.*
He’d avoided Leviathan because he was afraid. Then he’d made up a personal excuse to skip the launch ceremony because he didn’t want to face Jin Taekyung.
That might have kept him alive and in one piece. But once it was all over, something worse than death had been waiting for him.

└ Those guys really are something. That S-rank Hunter hasn’t shown his face once, even now, lmao. What was his name again? └ Genji. └ Isn’t it Hanzo? └ That’s Genji’s older brother. └ Are you guys insane? └ Why are you talking about a dead game from ages ago, you fossils? └ It’s true, though? Look it up if you don’t believe me. └ ? └ It’s real; he actually has an older brother named Yamamoto Hanzo. └ How is this real? └ So can Genji use Swift Strike? └ He’s great at Swift No-Show. └ LMAO └ Goddamn, that really hurts my pride. └ wwwwwww I was about to get mad, but I laughed without even realizing it? └ “Don’t laugh at him too much, okay? I thought it was kind of funny, though.” wwwww └ Even wasabi’s laughing, lmao. └ Lmao, wasabi showed up, but where’s the black bean sauce? └ It’s now confirmed that Jin Taekyung is from Shanxi Province, China. After examining old historical records, renowned historians at Peking University discovered the Jin Family of Taiyuan (see more) └ The second they see an opening, these bastards launch straight into their Jin-is-Chinese campaign. └ Didn’t the Red Guards destroy their old records? └ (This comment has been hidden.) └ So did Genji—or was it Hanzo—actually go to the Middle East this time? └ Yeah. I heard they accepted him since he’s an S-rank Hunter, at least. └ Isn’t he just going to sit out the fighting? Doesn’t seem like he’d be much help anyway. They should just send him around to entertain the troops. └ Captain Wasabi.
*How dare they? How dare they insult me—Genji—like that?*
Remembering the comments, Yamamoto shuddered.
Swift No-Show. Captain Wasabi.
The more he turned those words over, like awls digging into his lungs, the more his rage made him tremble.
And on top of that...
*That rude reply? In front of the Self-Defense Forces?*

Jin Taekyung’s warning, which was practically a threat—and the way the Self-Defense Forces Hunters had hurried to hold Yamamoto back instead of getting angry at such rudeness—had stripped away every last bit of Yamamoto Genji’s pride.
*If I go back now, what does that make me?*

By all accounts, he was an S-rank Hunter. But everyone who’d heard the rumors looked down on him. He’d scoured the desert with everything he had, determined to change how they saw him, and it had looked as if he was about to get results.
And now, an emergency withdrawal order.
Yamamoto had been muttering curses under his breath nonstop when a suspicion struck him.
*That Chōsenjin... Could it be? No. Of course it is.*
That was it. All of this was Jin Taekyung’s scheme to stop him from earning credit. The anti-Japanese sentiment that had started long ago had followed him all the way here.
Having reached a conclusion that was practically a delusion, Yamamoto barked,
“Oi, sutoppu!”
At his sudden order to stop, the evacuation vehicle ground to a halt.
Unlike before they’d set out, when they’d strongly objected to disobeying the withdrawal order, the Self-Defense Forces Hunters now meekly followed his command. Yamamoto’s face brightened.
*That’s right. I’m the beacon of the great Yamato people! The one they follow isn’t that Korean—it’s me...!*
The thought broke off.
The Self-Defense Forces Hunters looked bewildered. At the same instant, a realization flashed through Yamamoto’s mind.
“Wait. Who’s in the driver’s seat?”
One of the Self-Defense Forces Hunters blinked and answered,
“No one.”
“Eeh?”
“It’s an unmanned vehicle.”
Silence fell.
They stared at one another, then understood why the vehicle had stopped when it had been driving along just fine.
And why they could no longer hear the rain that had been pouring all around them.
“Ambu—!”
“Ambush!”
And at the same time—
*BOOM!*
A tremendous roar and impact engulfed them.

└ Those guys really are something.
That S-rank Hunter hasn’t shown his face once, even now, lmao.
What was his name again? └ Genji. └ Isn’t it Hanzo? └ That’s Genji’s older brother. └ Are you guys insane? └ Why are you talking about a dead game from ages ago, you fossils? └ It’s true, though?

Look it up if you don’t believe me. └ ? └ It’s real; he actually has an older brother named Yamamoto Hanzo. └ How is this real? └ So can Genji use Swift Strike? └ He’s great at Swift No-Show. └ LMAO └ Goddamn, that really hurts my pride. └ wwwwwww I was about to get mad, but I laughed without even realizing it? └ “Don’t laugh at him too much, okay?

I thought it was kind of funny, though.” wwwww └ Even wasabi’s laughing, lmao. └ Lmao, wasabi showed up, but where’s the black bean sauce? └ It’s now confirmed that Jin Taekyung is from Shanxi Province, China.

After examining old historical records, renowned historians at Peking University discovered the Jin Family of Taiyuan (see more) └ The second they see an opening, these bastards launch straight into their Jin-is-Chinese campaign. └ Didn’t the Red Guards destroy their old records? └ (This comment has been hidden.) └ So did Genji—or was it Hanzo—actually go to the Middle East this time? └ Yeah.
I heard they accepted him since he’s an S-rank Hunter, at least. └ Isn’t he just going to sit out the fighting?
Doesn’t seem like he’d be much help anyway.
They should just send him around to entertain the troops. └ Captain Wasabi.
*How dare they?
How dare they insult me—Genji—like that?*
Remembering the comments, Yamamoto shuddered.
Swift No-Show.
Captain Wasabi.
The more he turned those words over, like awls digging into his lungs, the more his rage made him tremble.
And on top of that...
*That rude reply?
In front of the Self-Defense Forces?*

Jin Taekyung’s warning, which was practically a threat—and the way the Self-Defense Forces Hunters had hurried to hold Yamamoto back instead of getting angry at such rudeness—had stripped away every last bit of Yamamoto Genji’s pride.
*If I go back now, what does that make me?*
By all accounts, he was an S-rank Hunter.
But everyone who’d heard the rumors looked down on him.
He’d scoured the desert with everything he had, determined to change how they saw him, and it had looked as if he was about to get results.
And now, an emergency withdrawal order.
Yamamoto had been muttering curses under his breath nonstop when a suspicion struck him.
*That Chōsenjin...
Could it be?
No.
Of course it is.*
That was it.
All of this was Jin Taekyung’s scheme to stop him from earning credit.
The anti-Japanese sentiment that had started long ago had followed him all the way here.
Having reached a conclusion that was practically a delusion, Yamamoto barked,
“Oi, sutoppu!”
At his sudden order to stop, the evacuation vehicle ground to a halt.
Unlike before they’d set out, when they’d strongly objected to disobeying the withdrawal order, the Self-Defense Forces Hunters now meekly followed his command.
Yamamoto’s face brightened.
*That’s right.
I’m the beacon of the great Yamato people!
The one they follow isn’t that Korean—it’s me...!*
The thought broke off.
The Self-Defense Forces Hunters looked bewildered.
At the same instant, a realization flashed through Yamamoto’s mind.
“Wait.
Who’s in the driver’s seat?”
One of the Self-Defense Forces Hunters blinked and answered,
“No one.”
“Eeh?”
“It’s an unmanned vehicle.”
Silence fell.
They stared at one another, then understood why the vehicle had stopped when it had been driving along just fine.
And why they could no longer hear the rain that had been pouring all around them.
“Ambu—!”
“Ambush!”
And at the same time—
*BOOM!*
A tremendous roar and impact engulfed them.

chapters.title: Chapter 797
paragraphs: In just a few days, the main force had built a solid command structure and amassed tremendous fighting strength.

The World Hunter Federation had led the way. The major powers of the G20 were among the first to lend their strength, and even the UN peacekeeping forces, forged into elite troops by the Great Cataclysm, had joined them.
The people gathered in the strategy room were the head and limbs that moved this enormous body.
Chuck Hagel had listened to my explanation in silence. Now he spoke slowly.
“That fucking terrorist has been covering Michael Silbert’s ass from the very beginning?”
I nodded without hesitation.
“Yes.”
“You believe him? Huginn, I mean.”
“Am I crazy? I wouldn’t trust a bastard like that.”
“Then what do you believe?”
“His fear.”
Chuck Hagel studied me for a moment, then tapped the ash from his cigar.
“Sounds like it’s true.”
“At least, that’s how it felt to me.”
“You’re sure?”
“Not a hundred percent. Maybe ninety-five. Even Huginn has no reason to lie in a situation like this.”
“What about the other five percent?”
“The people visiting him with knives in hand are filling that in. Maybe we’re up to ninety-seven by now.”
The first confession was the hard part. After that, it got easier. Now that Huginn had started talking, he’d drag out everything he knew—even things he’d forgotten.
Pain wasn’t what broke a strong person. It was the fear inside them.
*Of course, he’ll be tortured plenty before then.*
Everyone here probably knew what was happening, but no one said it aloud.
What mattered now wasn’t Huginn, who was probably being reduced to a bloody mess. It was what we did next.
We had to make a new plan on the assumption that everything he’d confessed was true. The Prophet wasn’t just some lunatic terrorist. He was strong enough to kill a Grand Mage on his own.
“How strong do you think he is?” Team Leader Choi asked cautiously.
Chuck Hagel smacked his lips. “Hard to say. We know next to nothing about him.”
“Mr. Hagel, this may be an impolite question, but if you’d been in The Prophet’s position and targeted Siegfried Bassmann, how would you have fared?”
“I’d met Siegfried. We weren’t close, but I could’ve taken him out easily. For someone he didn’t know, though? Given how reclusive he was, it would’ve been close to impossible.”
“Then could it be...”
“It’s one of two things. Either The Prophet was so strong that Siegfried couldn’t even defend himself properly, or...” Chuck Hagel paused. “He was someone Siegfried had met before.”
The strategy room went cold.
The weight of what Chuck Hagel had said stunned everyone. We didn’t know which possibility applied to The Prophet. Either way, we were dealing with someone far stronger than we’d expected.

“Jin was right to call the search teams back,” Hagel said. “If they stayed scattered, they’d be easy to pick off one by one. Of course, if The Prophet is that strong, gathering a few hundred people might not help.”
He was right. Even among S-rank Hunters—practically strategic weapons in their own right—there were clear differences in strength.
It was unlikely, but if The Prophet was comparable to Michael Silbert, it would take three average S-rank Hunters attacking together, backed by a supporting force, to bring him down.
*The problem is, where the hell did someone that strong come from?*
No matter how I looked at it, I couldn’t figure it out.
The World Hunter Federation had already cleaned house and accounted for the whereabouts and circumstances of every living S-rank Hunter and every other major Hunter.
*He’s not an insider. So what is he?*
An unknown outsider. And from what Huginn had told me, an outsider who’d appeared no more than five years ago.
Huginn had first seen The Prophet three years ago, but he’d last seen the fourth Muninn five years ago.

Siegfried Bassmann, meanwhile, was a veteran among veterans who’d fought countless battles during the Great Cataclysm. He might have been a scholarly mage, but no one earned the title of Grand Mage through books and research alone.
However talented The Prophet was, there should have been an unbridgeable gap between them. Some kid who’d dropped out of the sky a few years ago couldn’t overcome a gap like that.
Except...
I was living proof that it could be done.
“The System...?”
“Hm?”
“Nothing. Just talking to myself.”
Chuck Hagel raised an eyebrow. I acted like nothing had happened and changed the subject.
“Anyway, how’s the withdrawal going?”
Team Leader Choi answered. “More than seventy percent of the search personnel have returned.”
“Faster than I expected.”
“We mobilized every means of transport we have. We’ve also informed Magic Johnson, Faye Chen, and Prince Felix of the situation and made the withdrawal of all search teams their top priority.”

This was the operations headquarters, but the others each commanded a force of their own according to their abilities. We’d had to spread out to search this vast region thoroughly. Making every team travel thousands—sometimes tens of thousands—of kilometers back here whenever it needed to return would have been stupid.
“All of Team A1 has returned.”
“Team B2 is still on its way back. We expect them within fifteen minutes and remain in contact.”
“We’ve temporarily lost contact with Team D4. We suspect interference from magical power and have dispatched a support team as a precaution.”
Reports poured in from all around the room, starting with Team Leader Choi.

Some search teams under headquarters command hadn’t returned yet, and others were out of contact. For now, though, there was no reason to worry. As magical power levels rose, mana communications and radio signals naturally grew less reliable.
And even if something like a Monster Wave happened, *that guy* could handle it.
Beep.
—Emergency transmission, emergency transmission. This is Team F6. A monster army has appeared ahead. The monsters appear to be undead. Requesting support.
Team Leader Choi and I met eyes and sighed at the same time.
“Tell them not to attack.”
“Uh, they’re probably on our side.”
Chuck Hagel had sprung to his feet the moment the radio sounded. Now he looked as though he’d bitten into something foul.
“Damn it. Is it the guy I’m thinking of?”
“Yes. Judging by Team F6’s current coordinates, it’s definitely him. They must’ve gotten confused.”
“Tell him not to scare the troops. Plenty of them haven’t seen him in person. We don’t need the confusion.”
“The Skeleton King will take that into account, so there’s no need to worry too much—”
Beep-beep!
—Emergency transmission! Emergency transmission! There are too many monsters! There’s a boss, possibly a named monster, and it’s laughing like a maniac! It’s terrifying! Requesting support!
Chuck Hagel gave us a flat look.
Team Leader Choi glanced away and muttered as if to himself, “No one will get hurt. Probably...”
“That last word didn’t sound very confident. Am I imagining things?”
“Yes.”
I let out a long sigh.
I’d sent that bastard to bring the troops back, and now he was scaring them instead.
Judging by the looks on the faces of the commanders seated around us, they were wondering whether we ought to deal with the Skeleton King before The Prophet.
*You’re dead when you get back.*
Just as I muttered to myself, another urgent transmission rang out.
Beep.
—Engagement in progress! Engagement in progress!
“Again?”
He was *really* dead.
But as I wondered how I could deal with the Skeleton King in a way that would make the story of his getting his ass kicked spread far and wide, an unexpected follow-up crackled in my ear.
—This is Team J1! Multiple dead! Multiple injured! Send support as fast as you can, aaagh!
Crunch. Splaash!
A chill ran down my spine.
The gruesome sound of flesh tearing and that scream came through the radio. Everyone in the strategy room, myself included, sprang to their feet.
“Fuck!”
“Find the transmitter’s coordinates! Now!”
“Sound the alarm! Dispatch the nearest search team to those coordinates immediately!”
“Teams P3 and P4 are moving within thirty-five kilometers!”
“Get the orders out! Hurry! And request support from the Skeleton King, too!”
Wheeeee!
The alarm blared through the speakers and spread into the darkness.
I threw myself out the open window and shot high into the air. A flash lit up the distance. I drew up my internal energy.
Bang!
The wind rushing past me seemed to carry the metallic scent of blood.
Whoosh. Boom!
Bone and flesh burst apart with a heavy rush of air.
The headless corpse dropped to its knees, and furious shouts erupted from every direction.
“No! Haruka!”
“You bastard! How dare you!”
Shing, shing, shing!
Blades swept through the darkness, cutting through sand thrown up by the force of their swings. They drove toward the enemy who had killed their precious comrade.
They thought they could cut him to pieces.
Then the sand beneath their feet surged upward, became enormous spikes, and pierced their bodies.
Thud! Crunch!
“Ghk.”
Their final gasps escaped as dark red blood soaked the sand.
Hundreds dwindled to a hundred, then a hundred to dozens, in little more than ten minutes.
Those who watched it happen trembled with fear that reached their bones. S-rank Hunter Yamamoto Genji was no exception.
*This... This can’t be real.*
People could call him Swift No-Show or an S-rank janitor, but he was still a veteran Hunter who’d fought his share of battles.
Even Yamamoto had never seen a fight this brutal or this one-sided.
Overwhelming power. Destruction. Terror.
No word he knew could describe the gulf between them.
He was too frightened to run. Too frightened even to swing the sword he’d drawn.
“What... What the hell are you?”
Slice!
An invisible wind cut down another person in place of an answer.
The tank who’d charged forward with a scream split in two, massive Tower Shield and all. Blood sprayed through the air, vivid even in the dark.
Splaash. Thud-thud!
Deep night. Dim moonlight.
A lone figure stood amid blood falling like a sudden downpour.
Rustle.
The hem of a long robe brushed the blood-soaked sand as the figure turned. Yamamoto Genji suddenly realized who had ambushed them.
“The... The Prophet...!”
Beneath the low-drawn hood, the figure’s lips curved gently upward.
The Prophet thrust out both hands and raked them down through the air like claws.
Whoosh! Slice!
Had space itself warped, or had he imagined it?
Yamamoto looked around in a daze. Corpses lay everywhere: faces gone, holes punched through chests, limbs severed.
Before he knew it, he was the only one left alive.
For the moment.
*I’m going to die. I know it.*
The fear of death was the one thing everyone shared.
Step.
Yamamoto took a step back without realizing it. He didn’t notice the sword hilt slipping from his sweat-slick hand.
No. He didn’t care.
If only he could survive. If only he could make it back to Japan alive.
But the next moment, someone’s unfamiliar voice pierced his ear.
“Where are you going in such a hurry, foolish servant?”
Just as Yamamoto Genji froze like a statue—
“Over there!”
“Someone’s there!”
“Get into formation!”
Vrooom.
Transport vehicle engines and people’s shouts sounded from every direction.
